units.translation: The figurative use of the word is manifold, as discussed in Thes. vol. 6 p. 2168, and several examples are found in Aeschylus, partly of the simple substantive, partly of the adjective compounded with πτερόν [wing], ὁμόπτερος [of the same wing]. The first example is uncertain, in verses which, as it seemed to me and others, are interpolated, Sept. 675 ἐχθρὸς σὺν ἐχθρῷ στήσομαι. φέρ᾽ ὡς τάχος κνημῖδας, αἰχμῆς καὶ πετρῶν προβλήματα [I will stand enemy against enemy. Bring quickly greaves, defenses against spear and stones], where in many copies αἰχμήν [spear] is written for αἰχμῆς [of the spear] and πτερῶν [of wings] for πετρῶν [of stones], about which Thomas Magister writes thus: τὰ προβλήματα τῆς αἰχμῆς ἤτοι τὴν αἰχμὴν, περιφραστικῶς, ἣν προβαλλόμεθα εἰς μάχην. γράφεται καὶ πτερῶν. καὶ τὸ μὲν πετρῶν εἴποις οὕτως, τὰ προβλήματα τῶν πετρῶν ἤτοι τὴν ἀσπίδα, ἣν προβαλλόμεθα τοῦ σώματος, καὶ δι᾿ ἧς τοὺς ἐκ πολεμίων ἡμῖν ἐπιόντας λιθασμοὺς δεχόμεθα. τὰ δὲ πτερῶν προβλήματα τοὸς ὀϊστοὺς νόει. [the defenses of the spear, that is, the spear, periphrastically, which we hold before us in battle. It is also written πτερῶν [of wings]. And you might say πετρῶν [of stones] thus: the defenses of the stones, that is, the shield, which we hold before our body, and by which we receive the stones coming at us from the enemy. But understand the defenses of πτερῶν [of wings] as arrows.] And the scholiast of the Vossian codex: γρ. αἰχμὴν, ἵν᾿ ἦ οὕτως· φέρε ως ὡς τάχος καὶ ταχέως τὰς κνη κνημίδας ας καὶ τὴν αἰχμὴν καὶ ἕνεκα τῶν πετρῶν τὰ προβλήματα, ἤτοι τὰ σκουτάρια [read αἰχμήν [spear], so that it is thus: bring quickly and speedily the greaves and the spear and for the sake of the stones the defenses, that is, the shields], and it must be admitted that πτερῶν [of wings] is recommended by the fact that it would be strange, as Hermann pointed out, for stones to be mentioned, which were used rarely and by chance in battles, while weapons, whose use was constant, were omitted. The same reasoning applies to the Euripidean passage Hel. 76, where Teucer speaks, εἰ δὲ μὴν ξένη | γαίᾳ πόδ᾽ εἶχον, τῷδ᾽ ἂν εὐστόχῳ πτερῷ | ἀπόλαυσιν εἰκοῦς ἔθανες ἂν Διὸς κόρης [but if I had set foot on foreign soil, you would have died by this well-aimed wing, a loss to the image of Zeus's daughter], in which πτερῷ [wing] is read for πέτρῳ [stone] from Elmsley's conjecture, deservedly approved by Hermann. For it was fitting for Teucer, famous for the bow, with which he undoubtedly appeared equipped on stage, to threaten arrows, not stones. And aptly is an arrow called πτερόν [wing], as arrows and darts are called πτερόεντες [winged] by poets, and Aeschylus himself (fr. 129) used πτέρωμα [plumage] of arrows. No less easy is the explanation of what is said of the Athenians at Eum. 1002, Παλλάδος ὑπὸ πτεροῖς ὄντας ἅζεται [he reveres those who are under the wings of Pallas], i.e. living under the protection of Minerva, the comparison drawn from birds covering their chicks with their wings. More boldly it is said at Suppl. 328 αἰόλ᾽ ἀνθρώπων κακά· πόνου δ᾽ ἴδοις ἂν οὐδαμοῦ ταυτὸν πτερόν [the varied evils of men; nowhere would you see the same wing of toil], as it is read from Turnebus's emendation for πότερον [which of two], i.e. that the appearance of all things that can happen to men is not the same. Very similar to this is what Zenobius Proverb. 6, 1 (copied by Photius and Suidas) noted, φόνου πτερόν [wing of murder]: the winged or swift one through arrows. But it is better to understand φόνον [murder] periphrastically: which Leutschius pointed out also has the character of Aeschylean diction. On the figurative use of the adjective ὁμόπτερος [of the same wing] we have spoken under that word.
For the four-legged bird skims the smooth path of the air with its wings.
